title: Hinterland Bank - Data Residency Discovery
summary: Intro discovery focusing on data residency, logging controls, and options between Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments. Customer is regulated financial institution; primary constraints: EU/US data residency, strict logging retention rules, auditability, KMS key control, and SOC2/ISO requirements. Agreed next steps: send security brief, propose Dedicated sizing, schedule technical deep dive for on-prem / VPC setup, and run a short benchmark with synthetic PII data.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
next_steps: Mark (Redwood) - Send security whitepaper + SOC2/ISO reports by 2026-05-21
Priya (Redwood) - Schedule technical deep dive (separate 60m) with Engineering team by 2026-05-26
Liam (Redwood) - Provide Dedicated sizing estimate and pricing sheet by 2026-05-22
John (Hinterland) - Share expected QPS, avg sequence length, and sample compliance checklist by 2026-05-21
action_items: Mark Turner - Share Hosted vs Dedicated pricing + SLA PDF - due 2026-05-22
Priya Natarajan - Prepare VPC/private deployment diagram + KMS integration notes - due 2026-05-25

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Mark (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood CSM), John (Hinterland CTO), Sarah (Hinterland Compliance), Emily (Hinterland Infosec), Ben (Hinterland Platform)

[00:00] Mark (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Mark Turner, account exec for Redwood Inference. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer, and Liam from customer success. How are you all?

[00:12] John (Hinterland): Doing well, thanks. We appreciate the time. We've been evaluating options for serving LLM features and want to make sure we meet our data residency and compliance needs.

[00:24] Mark (Redwood): Totally. Today we wanted to understand your constraints - residency, logging, encryption, that sort of thing - and then walk through Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs. Priya will jump into technical questions.

[00:37] Priya (Redwood): Hi all. Quick question to start: where do you need data to reside? Is this EU-only, or US-only, or both? Any particular regions or legal entity separation?

[00:47] Sarah (Compliance): We have customers in both the EU and US. For EU customers we need data residency in the EU, obviously GDPR applies. Some of our corporate accounts also require that credit-card or payment tokens never leave our internal network. We also have strict logging retention rules - certain logs must be retained for seven years, others masked sooner.

[01:10] Emily (Infosec): To add, we have a SOC2 report and ISO 27001 scope, and any vendor handling personal data needs to be able to provide audit logs and evidence for encryption at rest and in transit. Key control is a big deal for us - we prefer customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM).

[01:28] Priya (Redwood): Understood. For hosted customers we offer regional endpoints and can restrict processing to EU regions, but there are caveats around logs and support artifacts. For Dedicated you get reserved capacity in a region and stronger isolation; for Private we can run in your VPC or on-prem for full control including customer-managed KMS.

[01:50] Ben (Platform): What exactly do you log in Hosted? We cannot have raw PII stored in a vendor-accessible log for more than 30 days without masking.

[02:02] Mark (Redwood): Good question. On Hosted we retain request/response logs for up to X days for debugging and SRE, but there are configurable retention policies. We offer PII redaction tooling and can configure shorter retention windows. That said, for customers with strict retention or zero vendor-visible PII, Dedicated or Private is typically recommended.

[02:22] Sarah (Compliance): So are you able to offer a guarantee that EU-origin data never traverses out of EU on Hosted? Our legal team will want that in writing.

[02:34] Priya (Redwood): We can guarantee processing within EU regions when you route to an EU endpoint; however some control-plane metadata and tooling access may still be in our control plane depending on the deployment. With Dedicated deployed in an EU cloud region we can keep both control and data plane regional. For full legal isolation we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem).

[02:58] John (CTO): Performance is also a factor. We don't want latency regressions for EU users if we pin everything to EU. How much difference are we talking about between Hosted EU endpoints and a local Dedicated cluster?

[03:14] Priya (Redwood): Typically hosted EU endpoints are low latency for EU clients - within 30-60 ms depending on model size and seq length. Dedicated in same region has similar latency but gives you guaranteed throughput and no noisy neighbors. Private on-prem could add variability depending on your infra. We can run a benchmark with your sample P95 latencies.

[03:40] Emily (Infosec): About KMS - if we bring our own key, do you support HSM-backed keys and can Redwood access them for debugging or only customer admins?

[03:52] Mark (Redwood): We support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated and Private. With Hosted we integrate with cloud KMS options and can work with HSM-backed keys, but vendor access depends on the agreement. For Dedicated/Private we operate under an RBAC model where Redwood SREs can be restricted; we can provide audit trails for key usage.

[04:15] Ben (Platform): What about model caching and logs? We do prefix caching and store KV caches - are those treated as logs or ephemeral?

[04:27] Priya (Redwood): KV cache is ephemeral and kept in-memory for performance; not persisted as logs. However debug snapshots for root cause analysis can be captured; those would be considered logs and subject to retention policies. For strict controls we can disable snapshotting or ensure snapshots never leave the customer's VPC in Private mode.

[04:50] Sarah (Compliance): We need to be very clear about what Redwood staff can see. Our security policy says no vendor personnel should be able to see raw customer prompts or responses containing PII.

[05:03] Mark (Redwood): Understood. We have controls to mask PII before it reaches Redwood logs and to disable request logging for sensitive routes. For enterprise Dedicated and Private we can implement stricter RBAC and require just-in-time access with approvals.

[05:22] John (CTO): Ok, walk me through the practical differences when it comes to incident response and auditability. If an auditor asks for logs for a six-month window, what do you provide?

[05:34] Priya (Redwood): We can provide structured audit logs that show API calls, timestamps, and key identifiers. For Hosted customers, we provide aggregated logs and access via our console and can export logs to your SIEM. For Dedicated, we can provide direct log streams or S3 exports in-region. For Private, logs stay in your environment and are subject to your retention. We retain control-plane logs longer per contract.

[06:02] Emily (Infosec): Can logs be pushed to our Splunk/ELK without retention on Redwood side? We want canonical copy in-house and minimal vendor retention.

[06:14] Mark (Redwood): Yes, we support log forwarding and can reduce or eliminate vendor-side retention per agreement for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted there are limits but we can usually reduce retention to meet stricter SLAs for enterprise customers.

[06:33] Ben (Platform): Encryption in transit pretty standard, TLS. But what about internal encryption between services in your hosted stack? If data is processed across microservices in different AZs, is it re-encrypted?

[06:45] Priya (Redwood): We encrypt in transit end-to-end and we also encrypt at rest. Internal service-to-service calls are authenticated and use mTLS. For Dedicated/Private we can support customer-supplied certs and additional network restrictions.

[07:02] Mark (Redwood): One practical approach we've seen work is: for EU GDPR folks, route EU traffic to EU dedicated cluster and use request-level redaction for PII before sending into logs; for the most stringent customers we recommend Private with customer-managed KMS and S3/logging under their control.

[07:20] John (CTO): What about HIPAA? We have a small line of business that might handle PHI down the road. Is Redwood willing to sign a BAA and handle PHI?

[07:31] Mark (Redwood): We do support HIPAA customers and can sign a BAA. Usually this goes hand-in-hand with Dedicated or Private deployments to ensure separation and key control. We'll share our compliance pack.

[07:45] Sarah (Compliance): Auditability: we need immutable logs. Can you support write-once storage for audit trails?

[07:54] Priya (Redwood): For Dedicated we can configure append-only storage in S3 with object lock in-region. For Private it's up to your infra, but we can integrate with whichever immutable store you use.

[08:10] Ben (Platform): On the engineering side, what's the effort to stand up a Dedicated cluster? Time to first test?

[08:18] Priya (Redwood): Typically 2-4 weeks for baseline capacity and networking, depending on cloud approvals. Private (VPC) can be 4-8 weeks if they require air-gapped on-prem with HSM procurement. We'll need network details and an infra contact.

[08:32] Mark (Redwood): John, could you share rough QPS and average sequence length? That will help us size Dedicated.

[08:40] John (CTO): For our chat features it's currently 8-10 QPS for peak, avg seq length ~350 tokens. For batch jobs (embeddings) it spikes occasionally to 40 QPS. We can share more precise telemetry after the call.

[09:01] Priya (Redwood): Great - with that profile a small Dedicated pool should handle it with room for burst. We'll include burst/buffer suggestions in the sizing.

[09:13] Emily (Infosec): One other question: model snapshots or checkpoints - who can download model artifacts? We can't have vendor employees exporting models that might be re-used outside contractual boundaries.

[09:25] Mark (Redwood): Models we host are either open models or ones you bring; access to model artifacts follows the deployment. For Dedicated we can restrict artifact access; for Private you control the images. We can put NDA/contractual clauses around artifact handling.

[09:40] Sarah (Compliance): If we go Hosted for agility, what's the fastest path to prove compliance to our legal team? A security questionnaire + SOC2 reports won't be enough, they'll want data flow diagrams and region guarantees.

[09:55] Mark (Redwood): We'll send a security deck, SOC2 report, ISO summary, and a data flow diagram for the hosted EU endpoint. But we should highlight the limitations: Hosted can meet many cases, but if legal insists on control-plane separation, Dedicated is the better fit.

[10:12] John (CTO): Are you able to accept inbound connections only from our VPC, like private endpoints?

[10:20] Priya (Redwood): Yes - for Dedicated and Private we support private link / VPC peering and private endpoints. For Hosted we offer IP allowlists and VPC peering in some regions but not all features are identical.

[10:34] Ben (Platform): We need to ensure no support tickets leak sensitive transcripts to Redwood support staff. Is ticketing integrated with transcripts?

[10:45] Liam (Redwood CSM): We can anonymize transcripts in support tickets and require you to attach redacted logs. For Dedicated/Private we can disable automatic transcript uploads to support systems.

[10:58] Sarah (Compliance): On logging retention, our policy: PII in logs must be masked within 24 hours; metadata can be retained 7 years. Can you support differential retention windows?

[11:12] Priya (Redwood): Yes, we can configure per-route retention and masking policies. We'll capture the policy you need and reflect it in the contract.

[11:27] John (CTO): Pricing question: Dedicated vs Hosted cost difference - any rule of thumb?

[11:35] Mark (Redwood): Hosted is pay-as-you-go, usually lower up-front but potentially higher unit costs at scale. Dedicated has a reservation/commit with lower per-token cost and guaranteed capacity. Private has license + infra + support fees. We'll send a comparative pricing sheet.

[11:52] Emily (Infosec): For the technical deep dive, we want to have our network and infra folks join. Can Priya cover VPC peering, IAM integration, and KMS specifics?

[12:03] Priya (Redwood): Absolutely. We'll prepare a diagram and sample CloudFormation/Terraform snippets for peering and IAM roles.

[12:14] Sarah (Compliance): Also need a sample clause for data residency and a BAA template.

[12:20] Mark (Redwood): We'll include a template BAA and suggested contract language.

[12:27] John (CTO): Curious about fallback: if Dedicated cluster in EU is exhausted, do you failover to US or degrade? That's a red flag for legal.

[12:36] Priya (Redwood): Failover policies are configurable. For EU legal constraints we can disable cross-region fallback. For availability we can set canary capacity or multi-AZ in-region. Fallback to another region would only happen with explicit permission.

[12:52] Ben (Platform): Any limitations on model sizes for on-prem? We run some larger LLMs internally.

[12:59] Priya (Redwood): On-prem sizing depends on your hardware; we support large models but will advise on GPU types and quantization profiles. For very large models you may need node-level memory adjustments.

[13:16] Mark (Redwood): Quick recap so we capture next steps: we'll send security docs, pricing and sizing, and schedule a technical deep dive. We'll also ask for your telemetry for sizing and your compliance checklist.

[13:30] John (CTO): Sounds good. If we get the security pack and the Dedicated pricing, legal and procurement will review. We'd like a pilot in EU-only Dedicated if possible.

[13:42] Mark (Redwood): Great. We'll prioritize the EU Dedicated plan for pilot. Priya will reach out to schedule the deep dive.

[13:50] Sarah (Compliance): One last quick: can you confirm log export formats? We use JSON lines to ingest to our SIEM.

[13:58] Priya (Redwood): We can export JSONL, and we support S3 push or direct syslog/Splunk forwarding.

[14:06] Mark (Redwood): Alright - thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items we discussed.

[14:12] John (CTO): Thanks, appreciate it.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: moderate; occasional mis-attributions and a few words unclear in noisy sections.
